title: Double one number, halve the other
practice: Try a few problems at your own pace, then return to any explanation you want to revisit.

sections.html:
Four small bags each hold six counters. Empty two bags into one larger bag, and do the same with the other two. You now have two larger bags, each containing twelve.

The amount is unchanged: 4 × 6 = 2 × 12 = 24. You halved the number of bags and doubled what goes into each bag. This is a repacking trick, not a new way to create counters.
sections.title: Repack the same objects

sections.html:
Draw six groups of five dots. Pair the groups, circling each pair together. You now have three groups of ten without adding or removing a dot.

For 6 × 5, pair the six groups into three groups of ten. Three tens are thirty, so 6 × 5 is also thirty. The second arrangement may be easier to count even though both show the same objects.
sections.title: Try it yourself

sections.html:
The two numbers in a multiplication are called factors. If you double one but leave the other unchanged, you double the total. The total stays the same only because the other factor is halved at the same time.

These examples use even numbers of groups so that halving produces a whole number of groups. Later, fractions let us discuss other cases. For now, keep the repacking concrete.
sections.title: Change both factors together

sections.html:
Consider 16 × 5. Halve sixteen to eight and double five to ten. Eight tens are eighty. You can check by adding sixteen five times, but the regrouping uses fewer steps.

This does not automatically make every multiplication easier. If the transformed numbers feel less familiar, keep the original calculation. The useful question is “which arrangement can I count confidently?”
